title: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — Section 148 (Bailment, bailor and bailee defined)

content.overview: Section 148 defines a bailment as the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The person delivering the goods is the bailor; the person to whom they are delivered is the bailee. The Explanation provides that if a person already in possession of the goods of another contracts to hold them as a bailee, he thereby becomes the bailee, and the owner becomes the bailor, although the goods may not have been delivered by way of bailment.
content.glance: Bailment is delivery of goods for a purpose on a contract that they will be returned or disposed of as directed when the purpose is accomplished. Bailor delivers; bailee receives. The Explanation covers constructive bailment where possession already exists and a contract to hold as bailee is made.
content.study: A ‘bailment’ is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them. The person delivering the goods is called the ‘bailor’. The person to whom they are delivered is called the ‘bailee’. Explanation.—If a person already in possession of the goods of another contracts to hold them as a bailee, he thereby becomes the bailee, and the owner becomes the bailor of such goods, although they may not have been delivered by way of bailment. Current-law framing: possession (not ownership) passes for a defined purpose with an obligation to return or deal as directed; the Explanation recognises bailment by contract without fresh physical delivery.

sections.heading: Definition of bailment
sections.body: A ‘bailment’ is the delivery of goods by one person to another for some purpose, upon a contract that they shall, when the purpose is accomplished, be returned or otherwise disposed of according to the directions of the person delivering them.

sections.heading: Bailor and bailee
sections.body: The person delivering the goods is called the ‘bailor’. The person to whom they are delivered is called the ‘bailee’.

sections.heading: Explanation — constructive bailment
sections.body: If a person already in possession of the goods of another contracts to hold them as a bailee, he thereby becomes the bailee, and the owner becomes the bailor of such goods, although they may not have been delivered by way of bailment.

examples.title: Repair of goods
examples.body: A delivers a watch to B for repair, on the understanding that it will be returned when repaired. This is a bailment: A is bailor, B is bailee.

examples.title: Constructive bailment under the Explanation
examples.body: B is already in possession of A’s goods. B contracts with A to hold them as bailee. B becomes the bailee and A the bailor, even without fresh delivery.

hypotheticals.question: A leaves goods with B for safe custody, agreeing they will be returned on demand. Is this a bailment?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes. There is delivery for a purpose (safe custody) upon a contract that the goods will be returned when the purpose is accomplished. A is bailor; B is bailee.

hypotheticals.question: B already holds A’s goods and then agrees to hold them as bailee. Does the Explanation apply?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes. The Explanation provides that B thereby becomes the bailee and A the bailor, although the goods were not freshly delivered by way of bailment.
